entry.title: Nvidia CEO Admits To Affair With An Accused Spy For The Chinese Government
entry.summary: On Sunday, Nvidia announced that it was opening an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang after he admitted to an affair with a Singapore-based data-center company executive named Alice Huang (no relation), whom U.S. officials say is also working as a spy for Chinese state intelligence. Given the size of Nvidia, as well as its strategic centrality to the intense AI buildout competition between the U.S. and China, Huang might be the single most desirable person in the tech industry, if not the whole world, for Beijing to honeypot. According to reporting around the matter, it seems like they got what they came for. We must begin with the crux of the issue, which is the matter of why Nvidia is in such a central position. AI software companies like OpenAI and Anthropic have gotten significantly more media attention because they make consumer products and engage in marketing rhetoric about their potential to create the machine god, but Nvidia is the company that has made the most actual money during the ongoing AI boom. Nvidia makes chips, supposedly the best of all the chips, on which every big-time software company built its flagship platforms a few years ago. This has made Nvidia the second-biggest publicly traded company in the world, and has made its founder Jensen Huang fabulously wealthy and quite the influential figure. It's also made the Santa Clara–based Nvidia the most critical part of the U.S. strategic plan to assert global AI dominance, by which I mean dominance over China, its principal competitor in the field. American trade policy forbids Nvidia from selling its best stuff to Chinese companies: U.S. policymakers want American companies to build the biggest and best data centers and create AI software that can most effectively and profitably book a flight for you, tell you some stuff you love about your kid, or conduct microtargeted drone assassinations of restive labor organizers.

entry.title: Marcin Borkowski: A tip on removing functions from hooks interactively
entry.summary: When I customize my Emacs, I often utilize hooks. However, when experimenting, I often inadvertently add the wrong thing to a hook – a function I later decide to rename or even a lambda. I have always painstakingly written the correct remove-hook invocation to do it. A few days ago it occurred to me that it would be nice to write an interactive wrapper around remove-hook to make it easier. As usual in such cases, I started with a bit of research to see if someone did something similar already. To my surprise, not only is this a solved problem, but it’s solved in Emacs itself! Apparently, almost six years ago remove-hook was made into a command and you can just M-x it, provide the hook variable name and use autocompletion to decide what to remove from it (including lambdas!). How cool is that?

entry.title: Patriots Emit Foul Odor In Blowout Loss To Packers
entry.summary: Things have to be really bad for the New England Patriots if even Christian Gonzalez is dropping a stinker. The All-Pro cornerback has been one of the most consistent players on a Pats team that has struggled to find consistency at other positions, but Sunday against the Green Bay Packers, Gonzalez was just like many of his teammates: overwhelmed and outmatched in a 45-27 loss that was functionally over by the third quarter. This was the worst performance of Gonzalez's pro career since he entered the NFL in 2023. Against Green Bay's receiving duo of Matthew Golden and Christian Watson, the league's highest-paid cornerback was helpless, consistently getting beat on deep routes and losing one or both in coverage for touchdowns. According to Next Gen Stats, Gonzalez gave up a total of 10 catches for 187 receiving yards on Sunday, the most of his career and the third-most of any player this season. He had given up a total of 196 receiving yards across his first six games. On Green Bay's second TD of the day, Gonzalez and teammate Marcus Jones both covered Watson as he ran to the corner, leaving Golden wide open. Late in the third quarter, Gonzalez over-leveraged toward the outside against Watson, who just ran a skinny post and essentially walked into the end zone to make the score 40-14. "I mean, they just got the best of me today,” Gonzalez said after the loss. “I mean, this is pro football. They got good receivers like every team. So, they got the best of me today. Move on from it and be ready for next week.” His head coach Mike Vrabel was a little more pointed in his postgame comments: "When your best players don’t play good, you don’t have much of a chance in this league. So, we expect a lot more. He expects a lot more. We need more from him and everybody else."

entry.title: Charles Choi: Announcing Burnish
entry.summary: Org mode is often celebrated for its ability to “write once, export anywhere.” With such power comes added complexity: Exporting a file requires the user to typically go through a multi-step process (e.g. C-c C-e <some char> <some other char>). If the user is concerned with previewing changes to their file, then another step of viewing the exported output is required. Having to do this repeatedly gets tedious fast. Such is the motivation for Burnish. Burnish is a new Elisp package I’ve made to automate the export and viewing of an Org file. It provides an Emacs minor mode (burnish-mode) that when enabled, does the following upon save of an Org file: Export the Org file to a specified export backend. View the exported output in another Emacs window or by external tool. Most all of the default backends provided by Org mode are supported by Burnish. That said, Burnish is highly configurable, allowing for users to define for themselves the export and view workflow for existing or third party backends. Read the Burnish User Guide to learn more about it. As it is new, feedback is always welcome. If you really find it useful, please show your gratitude by buying me a coffee. Burnish v1.0 is now available on MELPA.

entry.title: The Bears Beat The Bucs With One Hand Tied Behind Their Backs
entry.summary: Sunday night's Bucs-Bears game possessed the major ingredients necessary for a Chicago fan freakout. Franchise quarterback Caleb Williams looked lost for much of the action, throwing four interceptions and stalling on three second-half three-and-outs. The team as a whole, meanwhile, surrendered a first-half 17-3 lead, allowing the game-tying touchdown following a fumble in the final stages of the fourth quarter. But the concerns one would have about the Bears' offense feel relatively minor today, because despite all their errors, a buzzer-beating Cairo Santos field goal and a stout defensive performance allowed Chicago to notch their fourth straight win, 27-24, improving to 7-2 as they fight for first place in the NFL's toughest division. The first nine minutes at Soldier Field were a party. The Buccaneers, entering the game as clear underdogs but coming off their two best outings of the season, got steamrolled, allowing a pair of Williams TD passes while mustering just six yards of their own. From that point on, however, everything became a struggle. Williams chucked a pick near the end zone to conclude a drive, then tossed another on his very next chance when he tried and failed to loft the ball out of bounds to avoid a sack. Before halftime arrived, he'd gift a third pass to the defense, making a silly decision to just huck the ball forward under pressure. Watching from afar, it felt like Williams's early success had put him in a consequence-free mindset on the field, and in his postgame it did very much sound like confidence was the culprit. "I'm going to throw until I can't throw anymore," Williams said. "That's how I live. I work my tail off to be in this position. I'll never not throw the ball. I could throw 100 picks in one game. ... That's how I grew up. That's who I am. I don't get gun-shy."

entry.title: Why Wouldn’t NC State Hire Philip Rivers?
entry.summary: One imagines Philip Rivers in his fortress of solitude, away from his platoon of children and contemplating what to do with his winter now that his St. Michael Catholic High School team has been knocked out of the Alabama high school playoffs. Then it hit him: Well, if the Chargers won't ask me to replace Justin Herbert before he gets killed, maybe I'll just go coach North Carolina State. Of course, it didn't happen that way, because the former quarterback's name has been the one most linked with the Raleigh job since Dave Doeren got tagged and bagged in late October. The possibility of him stepping into the gig was the principal discussion point in Rivers's postgame presser after St. Michael lost to Glenwood School on Friday night. It had been considered the faitest of accompli for weeks, in fact, and Rivers had already been elevated to First Candidate In Training when his son Gunner (of course that is his name), who had been Rivers's quarterback at St. Mike's, committed to NC State. The presumption here is that Rivers's prosciutto-thin coaching résumé—in mentioning his six seasons at St. Mike, we have covered all of it—has been trumped by his ability to pry open donor pockets and make the Wolfpack relevant again in the bloated ACC. And when we say "again," we mean "as a big spender in a landscape where 'big' is $40 million a year rather than $20 million." Doeren made a point of describing the limitations that such a barebones budget played on the school's chances of being noticed, and the school responded with a simple, You're absolutely right about that, Dave-O. Now get out.

entry.title: Connor Hellebuyck Won’t Start In Winnipeg Because Of “Expected Win Probability”
entry.summary: Some of the most memorable nights in hockey are driven by malice. If the NHL could capture in a bottle the atmosphere of John Tavares's first trip to Long Island after signing with Toronto, or Brady Tkachuk's Ottawa return as a Panther, it could and would sell it. And fans would buy it, because what these nights are really about is catharsis: the purging of resentments and the reaffirmation of loyalties. It's a nice thing to do from time to time. Builds community. Strengthens fandom. Probably good for mental health. The crowd that boos together, cheers together. Winnipeg wants and deserves a night of catharsis, to wish a not-so-fond farewell to Connor Hellebuyck, the greatest player the franchise has ever had, and who got so sick of both losing and living in Winnipeg that he forced his way to New Jersey. And wouldn't you know it, the Devils are on a Canada swing, and will take on the Jets on Tuesday. It ought to be personality-driven appointment viewing, in a league that doesn't have nearly enough of that. But the Devils have affirmed their commitment to non-entertainment. Connor Hellebuyck will not start in Winnipeg, per an all-timer of an official statement.

entry.title: You Could Be County Clerk, Or Sheriff!
entry.summary: You—yes, you—could be in elected office today. The median Defector reader is a smart and good-looking progressive with impeccable taste. What other qualifications do you really need? Had you thrown your hat in ahead of the blue wave, today you could be your state's lieutenant governor. Hell, for that matter, maybe you are your state's lieutenant governor. Have you checked your mail? Consider the case of Sebastian Matta, a 19-year-old sophomore at Arizona State University. He has a 3.25 GPA, per the New York Times, and he lives at home with his parents. Starting in February, Matta will be the Superior Court Clerk of Maricopa County, which has a geographic area larger than New Jersey and a population larger than Oregon. Matta will lead a department that, according to Phoenix-area CBS affiliate KTVK, processes more than 16,000 documents per day and has an annual budget of $65 million. entry.title: Lars Ingebrigtsen: OK, OK, I’ll just use tmdb
entry.summary:
After last night’s post, I realised I was probably just getting too invested in somehow using imdb for the “who’s that actor, anyway?” command for my Emacs-based video player. Not only is it an extremely fragile setup that’s gonna stop working, but it’s also very slow — it takes half a minute to return the actor profile images. So I just implemented a tmdb API shim and then I ask it for the actor profile photo instead. tmdb doesn’t have as large a data base, but… The API is free (for non-commercial use) and is extremely easy to use. Things are now faster:
The main wait is from the response from the LLM — I’m using gemini-3.8-flash. I’ve tried gemini-3.1-flash-lite, and it’s much faster… but gives the wrong result most of the time. No, that’s not Roy Scheider, Gemini! So now the setup is less Rube Goldberguesque. Sort of: I hit a key on my li’l wireless keyboard.
It’s picked up by a Python script that listens for evdev events.
It uses emacsclient to notify the Emacs running on the TV machine.
Emacs there tells mpv to do a screenshot.
Emacs waits until the screenshot arrives on disc.
Emacs sends it to Gemini and says “who dis? JSON please”.
Gemini responds and Emacs then creates an SVG overlay with the actor name.
rsvg-convert converts to PNG and then imagemagick convert to BGRA.
Emacs asks mpv to display it.
Emacs asks tmdb for the actor profile URL and fetches the image.
If it gets a response, it then recreates the svg with the image embedded.
(repeat 8-9).
Couldn’t be simpler.

entry.title: Irreal: BYOK
entry.summary:
interesting post about BYOK. BYOK is a “writer deck”, a device exclusively for writing that has no distracting apps or even a connection to the Internet. The idea is that writers can’t get distracted when they reach a temporary block by escaping to social media or something similar; they have to push through the block and get on with their writing.
According to Martin, BYOK is better than most devices in its class but there are still problems. He doesn’t like the available fonts and the screen—as you can see from the picture in his post—is pretty small, about 6 lines depending on the font. That seems to me to amount to a rather uncomfortable working environment. Fortunately, I don’t usually find myself distracted when I’m writing.
Then there’s the matter of research. Very often you need to look something up when you’re writing and you can’t do that with something like BYOK so you need to switch devices, pulling you even further out of the flow. And as Martin observes, it’s not easy to integrate your notes either.
The deal buster for me, though, is the builtin editor. It’s not Emacs based and doesn’t even support Emacs keybindings for navigation. As I’ve repeatedly said—as recently as yesterday—I simply can’t comfortably write outside of Emacs anymore. Martin is a relative newcomer to Emacs but he’s already feeling the discomfort. Once the Emacs way sets in, he’ll be just like me and won’t consider doing serious writing outside of Emacs.
Even if I were subject to being distracted by the greater Internet, I would simply turn off my WiFi to produce what is effectively an Emacs based writer deck. One thing for sure, I’m not giving up Emacs and suffering a second rate writing environment.

entry.title: Irreal: Why Use A Word Processor When You Have Org?
entry.summary:
And now it’s all this, Dr Drang has a post on using TextEdit versus using Pages. He’s a Mac user, obviously, but that doesn’t matter so much. The real argument is over whether one should use a word processor or some sort of text based editor.
There can be no doubt on where I stand on the issue. The only time I can remember using a “word processor” of any type in the last 3 decades was when I had to collaborate on another author’s file as a technical editor1. As I’ve said before, whenever I write in anything other than Emacs, I feel like I’m in Bizarro World where nothing works as it should. That includes even things like iMessage which is why I tend to use emacs-everywhere for it and most other things.
Dr Drang is nominally the same. He says he almost never uses a Word Processor but sometimes for a one-off he thinks it makes sense to use a word processor rather than one of his LaTeX or Markdown templates. That seems backwards to me. Sure, maybe you don’t want to use a template for a technical report to write a quick note to your baby sitter but Pages or any other word processor is not the simple alternative. I’d simply use Org and export it to whatever format seems appropriate. Even if Dr Drang is not an Emacs user, he is a Markdown user so surely the easy thing for him to do is to dash off his quick note in Markdown.
Really, unless you have collaboration issues, there’s no reason to subject yourself to the horrors of a word processor.
Footnotes: 1
That post was so long ago that I was still using Groff instead of Org to typeset documents. I’ve done technical editing since then that also required a Word clone and the experience was no better.

entry.title: Irreal: A New Journelly Beta
entry.summary:
Journelly. I use it as my memo book to record my daily activities and random things that I want to remember. For example, if I see some article or ad in my browser, I can ask Safari to share it with Journelly and a Journelly entry is automatically made complete with a link to whatever it was I wanted to capture. Each entry contains a date/time stamp as well as the location of where the entry was made.
Best of all, Journelly keeps its data as an Org file so I can query or edit it in Emacs. Of course, Journelly has a search function but sometimes I want to do a more complicated search or even to just count the number of entries in the database (4361 as of right now). Having the database as an Org file means that my data is available on all my devices, even if that device is a Mac.
I’ve been using Journelly since March 2025, ever since it was in beta, and have never looked back. Lately, however, it’s been getting a bit laggy, something I put down to my large database. I was on the verge of truncating my active data to the most recent entries in order to improve performance when Álvaro Ramírez pushed a new beta—v1.5(4)—that completely solved the problem. Now Journelly performs just like it did when I started.
If you are an Emacs user and are using an iPhone/iPad, I can’t think of any reason why you wouldn’t want to use Journelly. It allows you to integrate your day-to-day note taking with the power of Org mode. Even if you aren’t an Emacs user, you’ll probably find Journelly useful. It can also save its data as a markdown file so you can still get all the benefits of an easily accessible and editable database even if you prefer another editor.

another step in the journey so many of are on: moving everything inside Emacs. Regular Irreal readers will recall that Ridenour is a Philosophy professor so he doesn’t have much need for high powered math tools but he does have to deal with grade calculations and various budget items. I’m tempted to install it but I’m reasonably proficient with Calc itself so I probably wouldn’t use it enough to make it worthwhile. Still, if Reverse Polish Notation is not your thing and you’d rather deal with normal infix notation, literate-calc-mode may be a good fit. entry.title: Randy Ridenour: Emacs Literate Calc Mode
entry.summary:
Soulver on the Mac.
I recently stumbled on Literate Calc Mode by Robin1 that does everything I was using Soulver for, and I now have one more reason to not leave Emacs. It’s in Melpa, so installing it is simple. Once required, it provides both literate-calc-mode and literate-calc-minor-mode. I find the minor mode particularly useful for Org mode scratch buffers. For example, I used it recently to sketch out some details for a conference funding request. In an Org buffer, I entered:
Expenses for February 2027 Baylor Trip
Hotel = 500 Parking = 10 Registration = 295 Mileage = 300 Meals = 200
Total = Hotel + Parking + Registration + Mileage + Meals
M-x literate-calc-minor-mode instantly changed it to this:
Expenses for February 2027 Baylor Trip
Hotel = 500 => Hotel: 500 Parking = 10 => Parking: 10 Registration = 295 => Registration: 295 Mileage = 300 => Mileage: 300 Meals = 200 => Meals: 200
Total = Hotel + Parking + Registration + Mileage + Meals => Total: 1,305
=> is not editable and displayed in a lighter shade. Changing one of the variable values results in an instant update of the total. It uses Calc, so it is able to do almost anything that Calc can do. So far, I’ve used it to plan travel expenses and to build material lists for woodworking projects. It works flawlessly and I’ve found it surprisingly useful to have a scratchpad that can automatically do the math.

entry.title: Charles Choi: Announcing mdired, or adding a chainsaw to Dired
entry.summary: The ability to mark items in GNU Emacs Dired allows for bulk operations on both files and directories. With marking, onerous tasks can be turned into a trivial ones. While default Dired has many bulk operation commands, not everything is covered. That is the motivation for mdired, an Elisp package which extends Dired with some SIMD-style commands. Using these commands fall into two steps: Mark the items of interest in Dired. Run the mdired command. mdired supports the following four commands: mdired-copy: copy a single file to multiple directories. mdired-do-command: run an Elisp command or named keyboard macro on multiple files. mdired-compile: run compile on multiple directories. mdired-byte-recompile: byte-compile selected files or directories. Refer to the mdired User Guide for more details on usage. Closing Thoughts Bulk operation commands are chainsaws. Use them with caution. That said, they are great for improvised workflows: “Here’s this file that I want copied to a bunch of directories.” “I want to do the same edit operation on this set of files. I’ve got a named keyboard macro ready to go on them.” “I want to run the same make command on a bunch of directories.” As mdired is new, I’m open to feedback on it. Let me know what you think. mdired v1.0 is now available on MELPA.

entry.title: Nicolas Cavigneaux: Leaving asdf for mise
entry.summary: I first tried mise while setting up Arch Linux on my Dell XPS 13. I was bringing over my Doom Emacs configuration, which used asdf.el, and considering how mise would fit into the same environment. Colleagues had already spoken well of it. What interested me was the possibility of simplifying runtime integration in both Fish and Emacs. If that worked on the Dell, I was considering the same change on my Mac. The useful test was inside the editor. I set up separate directories for Ruby 3.4 and 3.3, opened their Ruby files in Doom, and checked the version from each buffer. Each one used the Ruby selected for its directory. I also confirmed that Doom could find Node and npm, and that the Elixir tools were available. That gave me a working setup on Arch before moving my main Mac environment away…

entry.title: Irreal: Highlighting The Active Window
entry.summary:
marking the active window (update here ) so that it’s easy to pick it out from the other, inactive windows. I did that by making the mode line of the active window a distinct color instead of the slightly different shade of gray from the other windows. That’s worked out really well for me and I’ve never looked back.
Now Ray Zeitler over at Ray on Emacs takes another look at the problem and found a really nice solution. It’s a bit more in your face than mine so if you’re looking for something that makes the active window really stand out, you should take a look at his post. The TL;DR is that instead of changing the active window, he changes the background color of all the other windows.
Zeitler found his solution on a 10 year old Stack Exchange post so it’s pretty certain to work no matter what version of Emacs you’re using. The code is very simple and you can simply copy it to your init.el if you’re interested.
As I said, this solution seems a little aggressive to me so I doubt I’ll be implementing it but others may disagree. One thing for sure, it’s going to make your active window stand out. It’s a small enough change that you can try it out—say by copying it to your scratch buffer and executing it—to see if it’s something you’d like.
